HeatScape / Philadelphia field prototypeBuilt for the everyday walk.
WHAT'S REAL / WHAT'S NEXT

Behind this first version

This is a working geometry and routing prototype, not a validated heat-navigation service.

Connected now

OpenStreetMap building footprints and street/path connections, downloaded November 10, 2026. Heights come from OSM tags, floor counts × 9.8 ft, or an assumed 39 ft where missing. Click a building to inspect its source.

SunCalc computes the sun position. Flat-ground building shadows are sampled along network segments approximately every 33 ft. Both displayed shadows and route scores use this model. The model holds the selected time constant throughout the trip.

How routes are compared

Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest route. Seven sun-exposure penalties produce alternatives; each candidate is split where it meets the shortest route. A section is replaced only if it reduces estimated sun and stays within the extra time allowed for that section. This search does not guarantee the global minimum-exposure route. Distances exclude the short snap from a selected point to the nearest connected network node.

Important gaps

Road centerlines are often used instead of sidewalk geometry. Tree shade, terrain, building courtyards represented by OSM relations, live closures, entrance access, indoor cooling availability, and wheelchair accessibility are not modeled. Approximate height and geometry can change the results. The dashed Center City study area has building shadows. Trips outside that area use a citywide walking graph prepared with OSMnx and computed in Python.

Where AI comes next

No AI model runs in this version. The planned experiment compares imagery-based canopy segmentation with existing canopy data, then evaluates its effect on observed sidewalk shade and route selection. This prototype establishes the map and routing foundation for that experiment.
